Lesson 01

A coding agent edits a repository under rules

Why it matters

It can read, propose a plan, change files, and run commands. Your rules say which of those happen alone.

Try it: Diff review

Lesson
01 of 06
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Result
A diff plus a test
Not the result
The summary
Deny
Secret files

A coding agent is the loop from School 06 pointed at a codebase. Products in this category include Cursor, GitHub Copilot's agent modes, Claude Code, Codex-style agents, Aider, Continue, and Cline. They differ in interface. They share the risk: a model with a terminal and a write path.

Decide explicitly

  • Which directories it may read, and which it may write.
  • Whether it may run tests, and which command.
  • Whether it may install packages, change git config, or contact the network.
  • That it may not read secret files. Name them: .env, key stores, credential JSON.
  • That applying the result is a diff a person can read, not a silent commit to the main branch.

If you cannot answer those, you do not have an agent setup. You have a default, and defaults differ by product and drift over time. Read the product's current permission screen and write down what you turned off.

Practice

For a repository you know, write the allow and deny list: directories, commands, and files. Include .env on the deny list even if your project uses a different name.

Check

What is the result of a coding agent, the summary or the diff?

Show the answer

The diff, plus the test command you ran. The summary is a claim about them.

Lesson 02

Give the agent the files and tests that matter

Why it matters

A whole monorepo in the prompt is not context. It is noise.

Try it: Diff review

Lesson
02 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Point at
Module and test
If the command is unknown
Stop before editing
Search
Inside a step cap

Point the agent at the module, the failing test, and the interface it must not break. Name the command that proves success. If you do not know the command, finding the command is the task, and the agent should stop before editing.

Goal: Fix the empty-state copy in the invoice list.
Read: src/invoices/list.tsx, src/invoices/list.test.tsx
Do not edit: src/billing/
Done: npm test -- invoices passes, and the test covers the empty state.

Let it search when the relevant file is unknown. Keep the step cap small so search does not become a tour. When it names the files it will change, that list is the moment to redirect it.

Practice

Write a goal block in the shape above for a small change you understand. If you do not have a repo, use a fictional one and still name a test command.

Check

Why name a test in the goal?

Show the answer

Because that command is the done-check. A green test is evidence. A summary is not.

Lesson 03

Plan, edit, run, then stop

Why it matters

A plan you can reject is cheaper than a pile of edits you have to unwind.

Try it: Diff review

Lesson
03 of 06
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Cheap to reject
A plan
Then
Edit inside the allowlist
Always
Stop and show the diff
  1. The agent states which files it will touch and what it thinks is wrong.
  2. You correct the plan or accept it.
  3. It edits inside the allowlist.
  4. It runs the test command you named.
  5. It stops, whether the tests passed or not, and shows the diff.

Skipping the plan is sometimes fine for a one-line change you already specified. It is a poor habit for anything that crosses a module. 'Keep going until the tests pass' without a cap is how an agent refactors the neighborhood and calls it a fix.

A failed test is a successful stop if the step cap is near. Record the failure. Do not let a second, unrelated edit 'try something else' in the same unreviewed tree.

Practice

Add a step cap and a stop sentence to the goal block from 08-02. Example stop sentence: 'I hit 6 steps. Tests are red. No further edits.'

Check

When is it reasonable to skip the written plan?

Show the answer

When the change is small and you already named the file and the test. Not when the agent is still looking for the cause.

Lesson 04

Review the diff and the tests

Why it matters

Read the change as if a new teammate wrote it. Then run the same command they ran.

Try it: Diff review

Lesson
04 of 06
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Read
Every hunk
Rerun
The same command
Red flag
A deleted assertion

Review for behavior, not for style the linter can catch. Look for extra files, weakened assertions, deleted tests, new dependencies, and changes outside the goal. Look for secrets that were read and echoed into a comment or a log.

A short review pass

  1. Does every hunk serve the goal? If not, revert the hunk.
  2. Did a test get deleted or did an assertion change to match a wrong implementation?
  3. Did the dependency list change? That is a separate decision.
  4. Run the test command yourself. Do not accept 'I ran it' without the output in the trace.
  5. Run the adjacent tests the change could have broken.

Green tests can be gamed

An agent can edit the test until it passes. Treat a test diff as carefully as a code diff. The expected value should still describe the behavior you want.

Practice

Write five review questions you will ask of the next agent diff you see. Keep them specific enough that each is yes or no.

Check

The agent says the tests passed. What do you do?

Show the answer

Run the named command and read the output. Check that the tests still assert the behavior you wanted.

Lesson 05

Secrets, destructive git, and the network

Why it matters

The expensive mistakes are not bad indentation.

Try it: Guardrail sandbox

Lesson
05 of 06
Time
11 min
Level
Core
Expensive mistakes
Secrets, git, network
Not the focus
Indentation
Write
The deny list
  • Deny secret files. If one was read, treat the session as exposed and rotate anything that file held.
  • Do not allow git push, force-push, or commit to the default branch. A commit on a branch you can throw away is a different, still-reviewed action.
  • Do not allow commands that delete history, drop databases, or send mail.
  • Package installs and curl-to-bash are network and supply-chain actions. Ask first.
  • A command allowlist beats a 'be careful' sentence in the system prompt.

Put the deny list in the tool layer. A prompt that says 'never run destructive commands' loses to a tool that can run them and a document that says 'you must'.

Practice

Write the command allowlist for a lab agent: the test command, and nothing else. Add three commands that are always denied.

Check

Where does the deny list have to live to be real?

Show the answer

In the tool permissions, not only in the prompt.

Lesson 06

Use a coding agent on a team without shipping junk

Why it matters

Agree the permissions, the review, and what 'the agent did it' does not excuse.

Try it: Diff review

Lesson
06 of 06
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Agree
Permissions and review
Not an excuse
The agent did it
Keep
Plan and test output

Teams that get value from coding agents in 2026 treat them as fast teammates with a narrow role. The author of the change is still a person. The pull request explains the behavior, the test command, and any permission the agent was given.

  • One shared permission profile is better than everyone clicking through defaults.
  • Agent commits are labeled, and they are small enough to review.
  • Generated code is not exempt from the style, security, or licensing rules.
  • If the agent used a retrieved snippet, the license of that snippet still matters.
  • A metric worth having: review time and escape rate, not lines generated.

Lines generated is a vanity metric. A change that takes longer to review than it would have taken to write is not a win, unless it was a change people were avoiding for a tracked reason.

Practice

Write three lines a pull request should contain when an agent helped: the goal, the test command and result, and the permissions used.

Check

Who is responsible for an agent-written change that ships?

Show the answer

The person who reviewed and merged it. The agent is not an author of record.
